explanations.explanation: This feature fires on low-frequency short character sequences (often two-letter subword fragments), especially those marking proper-name stems or otherwise rare letter combinations across languages.

This neuron fires on quantification cues—words or tokens that signal amounts, degrees or frequencies (e.g. determiners “some,” “every,” intensifiers like “fully,” numerals, percentages or list-item markers). It flags expressions that encode “how much,” “how often” or “in what quantity.”

This neuron is a “discourse‐marker cue” detector.  It lights up on the function word (often a preposition or negation) that heads a little embedded clause or phrase—things like the “in” of “bear in mind” or “in spite of,” the “matter”/“how” of “no matter how,” the “of” in “part of,” or the “don’t”/“doesn’t” introducing an exception or concession.  In other words, it spots the lexical pivot that signals a subordinate, contrastive/conditional, or exception clause.

This neuron lights up on little “glue” words that link clauses—subordinating or coordinating discourse markers (so, when, although, on, to, don’t, etc.) that signal causal, temporal, concessive or conditional relationships between phrases.

This neuron is a contrast/exception signaler: it lights up on markers that introduce a concessive or “exception” clause (e.g. the “apart from” in “apart from that…,” or the “but are”/“if you are… but are…” in the placeholder pages).

This neuron fires on those little opaque alphanumeric “chunks” you see as unique IDs or codes—e.g. the last slug in a YouTube/Spotify URL, a product/model number, MD5‐style fingerprint, etc. It flags short, arbitrary letter‐and‐digit tokens that serve as identifiers.
This neuron is essentially a “new‐segment/sentence start” detector—it lights up on the very first content word when a writer kicks off a fresh paragraph or standalone post/review.

This neuron is essentially a “non-Latin script” detector.  It lights up whenever the model sees characters outside the basic Latin alphabet—e.g. Chinese Han characters, Korean Hangul or polite endings, Arabic/Persian letters, etc.

This neuron lights up on two-digit numeric tokens that serve as the trailing segment in highly structured fields—most notably the “MM” in time stamps (HH:MM pm) and the last two-digit block in phone-number formats.
This neuron spikes on “modal” and hedging language—words that introduce possibility, advice or hypothetical framing (e.g. might, should, would, possibly, better, warranted).
